title: Challenging fire weather returns to Pacific Northwest as crews battle destructive Spokane blazes | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Fire crews in Washington state working tirelessly tocontain destructive blazesin the Spokane area are preparing for a new bout of flame-fueling winds and intense heat that will arrive on Friday and continue through the weekend.

A short-lived reprieve from adverse weather over the past couple of days gave crews a chance to make considerable progress on taming the flames, but upcoming conditions threaten to undo some of that hard work or fan sparks into new blazes.

Acomplex of three firesnear Spokane in the eastern portion of the state have scorched more than 10,000 acres of land and destroyed hundreds of homes and structures since igniting on Saturday. At one point, the fires forced tens of thousands of people to evacuate — some have since returned to findtreasured memories turned to ashes.

And for those whose homes survived the fires but are in immediate affected areas, “it is going to be weeks before we can safely let you in,” Spokane County Sheriff John Nowels said during a news conference Thursday, warning of air quality concerns in the area.

Nowels said evacuations will remain in place due to the incoming fire conditions expected this weekend. “There will likely not be any changes to the evacuation zones until the weekend is over and this weather event has passed us,” he said.

If a fire were to break out in those areas, firefighters are not certain they would be able to evacuate residents without risking fatalities or injuries, he added.

Authorities havearrested and chargeda Spokane resident with first-degree arson in one of the fires. The manadmittedto igniting the blaze and more than two dozen others since last year, Thursday court documents show.

Fires aren’t just raging near Spokane: There are dozens of active blazes across the West, including Washington, Oregon and California. These are producing smoke that’s creating abysmal air quality in the Pacific Northwest at large. It’s the worst fire season in more than 30 years for both states, one fueled by human-caused climate change.

With no rain in the forecast, here’s what to expect from the wind and heat in the coming days.

Temperatures are starting to climb higher than recent days. Highs in the mid-90s are expected Friday in the Spokane area, though smoke might block out enough warming sunlight to prevent temperatures from getting quite as hot as forecast.

Fire danger will ramp up again during the day and remain elevated through at least Saturday. A red flag warning is in effect for both days in Spokane and other parts of eastern Washington. Red flag warnings are issued by the National Weather Service to warn of weather conditions that could lead to dangerous wildfire spread.

Winds will start to pick up again during the day Friday, when peak gusts of 15 to 25 mph are expected. These winds are strong enough to blow around embers and keep fire crews on their toes, but are nowhere close to the nearly 50 mph gusts that fueled the fires’ initial explosive spread last weekend.

High temperatures could reach the upper 90s on Friday, which is about 10 degrees hotter than normalduring the area’s hottest time of the year.

Winds will ease overnight, but another bout of stronger winds will arrive Saturday afternoon. High temperatures in the mid-90s and gusts up to 25 mph could make Saturday another challenging day for fire crews.

A similar rhythm is expected heading into Sunday, with winds slowing overnight Saturday and speeding back up to gusts of 15 to 20 mph during the day.

Daytime winds could continue to pick up periodically into early next week, but high temperatures will start to come down into the upper 80s.

“Those winds are going to heat up. It’s going to be very hot over the next couple of days … it’s certainly something that’s very concerning for those fire crews,” Maj. Gen. Gent Welsh, commander of the Washington National Guard, told CNN’s Omar Jimenez. “They want to get those containment lines in now before that wind hits.”

Almost 400 members of the guard are deployed across the state, Welsh said.

The hot and windy trend will not be confined to eastern Washington. Central Washington will likely see even stronger winds, with gusts up to 30 mph possible starting Friday.

Winds of that strength start to present a greater risk of erratic wildfire behavior and spread, and a red flag warning has been issued in central Washington for both Friday and Saturday.

Similar to Spokane, the windiest periods will be during the daytime from Friday through Sunday, with weaker winds each night.

Central and eastern Oregon will also deal with periods of gustier winds each day. Many areas where fires are already burning could see gusts up to 20 mph, while the lower Columbia River Basin in northern Oregon could get up to 35 mph.

Nearly 50 large fires are burning in Washington and Oregon — about half of the nationwide total,according to the National Interagency Fire Center.

Several fires are also raging in California, including the Gann Fire in the Sierra Nevada foothills, which has burned more than 10,000 acres since it ignited Monday and left one person dead.

On Thursday, Gov. Gavin Newsom declared a state of emergency for Calaveras County due to the fire. A man was arrested in connection to the blaze, which investigators believe was accidentally started by sparks from a chain saw, according to the Associated Press. The suspect toldCNN affiliate KCRAhe was using a chain saw to cut scrap wood to earn money for dinner with his wife for his birthday when it ignited.

Smoke and its literal chokehold on air quality continue to be the most widespread impact of the ongoing fires.

Air quality in the Pacific Northwest has reached unhealthy or very unhealthy levels since the start of the week.

Extensive amounts of smoke are being trapped in place by an intense area of high pressure stuck over the West. High pressure limits winds near the surface, which prevents the smoke from clearing out.

Thursday was another day of unhealthy air quality in the region before high pressure began to lose its grip on the region overnight, allowing winds to return.

The same winds that could challenge fire crews through the weekend could also start to move some of the most stagnant smoke.

Air quality west of the Cascades in Seattle and Portland, Oregon, should continue to improve Friday as winds shift out of the west and push smoke east. Those same winds will keep parts of Washington and Oregon east of the Cascades shrouded in smoke, with poor air quality through the weekend.

Smoke higher in the atmosphere will also start to spread farther east, especially this weekend.

But this smoke is forecast to stay high enough that it’s unlikely to cause a repeat of thewidespread smoky conditionsand poor air quality that affected many areas in the central and eastern US in July.
